results.title: New tariffs test Georgia’s global trade resilience
results.content:
The White House initially established 10% tariffs on imports from all countries, along with higher “reciprocal” tariffs targeting nations such as China, Vietnam and members of the European Union that levy tariffs on U.S. goods. Mexico and Canada — Georgia’s top export destinations — were spared from the new tariffs. [...] Chinese tariffs could especially affect local businesses, the Georgia chamber noted. China was the third largest buyer of local goods last year at $3 billion, behind Canada and Mexico, and the second highest importer to Georgia at $17.2 billion.

On April 3, the chamber published a report outlining the impacts local industries may experience from the tariffs, including higher prices for car parts and steel, a squeeze on crop imports and possible slowdowns at the state’s bustling ports. [...] In 2024, the Peach State ranked seventh nationwide in net exports, shipping around $53.1 billion in locally made products overseas while importing about $145.6 billion, according to the Georgia Chamber of Commerce.

President Donald Trump’s newly unveiled tariffs have sent shockwaves through the manufacturing, technology and agricultural sectors across the country — particularly in Georgia.

results.title: Trump automotive tariffs, what’s at risk for the EV industry?
results.content:
In 2024, just over 1.5 million EVs were sold in the US market. Of these, 595,000 EVs were imported equating to 38% of all US EV sales in 2024 according to Benchmark’s EV Production Quarterly Outlook. These vehicles originated from 14 countries, with Mexico accounting for the highest number followed by Japan and South Korea.

#### Canada and Mexico will feel the tariffs, but have some leniency [...] While some vehicles manufactured in Canada and Mexico meet USMCA requirements, many do not, largely due to the globally integrated nature of EV supply chains. As a result, a significant number of vehicles originating from these countries will still be subject to tariffs, albeit at slightly lower rates compared to other countries.

#### Europe will feel biggest impact of automotive tariffs [...] In 2024, the US produced just over 1.1 million EVs, while the majority of these went to the domestic market, just under 186,000 EVs, 17%, were exported and sold outside of the country. Most of these vehicles, 57%, remained within North America going to the US’ neighbours Canada and Mexico. Outside of the region, US-made EVs had a limited market share. The next biggest destination was Europe which sold just over 60,000 US made EVs in 2024.
